uncited: This family of techniques estimates local ambient occlusion by querying a geometric representation—typically a Signed Distance Field (SDF) or a structured voxel grid—rather than performing explicit ray tracing against a triangle mesh or screen-space depth buffer.
By evaluating the distance to the nearest surface along specific directions, these methods approximate the visibility of the hemisphere around a point.

What sets this family apart from [JAOCC Shading](3634-jaocc-shading.md) (which uses precomputed spherical harmonics) and [Local Ambient Occlusion](4977-local-ambient-occlusion.md) (which often relies on screen-space or texture-based approximations) is the direct analytical or semi-analytical evaluation of geometric distance to determine occlusion factors.

All methods in this family rely on the fundamental property of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or structured geometry representations: the value at a point $p$ represents the shortest distance to the surface of the object, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the object.

The core mechanism for estimating ambient occlusion (AO) involves sampling the distance field along a set of directions, typically concentrated in the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal $\mathbf{n}$.
Let $d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v})$ be the distance to the surface in direction $\mathbf{v}$ from point $\mathbf{p}$.
The occlusion factor is derived by comparing these distances to the expected distance in an unoccluded environment.
A common formulation for the occlusion contribution of a single sample at distance $d$ is based on the ratio of the actual distance to the maximum possible distance or a reference distance.
For a hemisphere of radius $R$, if the distance to the nearest occluder is $d < R$, the point is considered partially occluded.

Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry emerged as a practical solution for real-time rendering where traditional ray-traced AO was too expensive.
The use of Signed Distance Fields for AO was popularized in the context of sphere tracing and voxel rendering.
These techniques are widely used in volumetric rendering, voxel games, and real-time graphics engines where geometry is represented implicitly or in structured grids.
